prompt: In an event-sourced system, what is the event log?

choices.text: An audit trail kept beside the real tables, in case somebody asks
choices.why: That is the picture the section replaces: here there are no other tables to sit beside.

choices.text: A cache of recent changes, cleared once they are applied
choices.why: Nothing is cleared; deleting an event would silently change a balance.

choices.text: The data itself
choices.why: Right. Any state on a screen was computed from it and can be computed again.

prompt: In the history of state_only.py, how many cents did Bia owe at the end of 24 March?
The library asks how much members paid in fines in March. Which version of state_only.py can answer?

choices.text: The history, by summing March's FinePaid events
choices.why: Right. The payments were recorded as facts; the balance only kept their net effect.

choices.text: Both, by subtracting the balances
choices.why: A balance mixes fines, payments and corrections; a payment cannot be told from a correction in a single number.

choices.text: Neither, because payments were never recorded at all
choices.why: The history has a FinePaid of 100 on 24 March.

prompt: Two clerks both read Bia's stream at version 2 and both append a loan. What does store.py do?

choices.text: Keeps both, since appending can never conflict
choices.why: Both would write version 3, and UNIQUE (stream, version) allows one.

choices.text: Locks the stream while the first clerk decides
choices.why: Nothing is locked; the conflict is found at the insert.

choices.text: Writes the first; the second gets ConcurrencyError and must re-read
choices.why: Right. Optimistic concurrency: the unique index refuses the second version 3.

choices.text: Merges the two loans into a single event, version 3, holding both copies
choices.why: A store never edits or merges events; the loser runs the rules again.

prompt: What stops an UPDATE on the events table in store.py?

choices.text: A trigger that raises "events are append-only"
choices.why: Right. The promise lives in the database, so it holds for any code that connects.

choices.text: The EventStore class has no update method
choices.why: True but not enough: the demo sends the UPDATE through store.db directly, and only the trigger stops it.

choices.text: SQLite refuses updates to tables with an AUTOINCREMENT key
choices.why: SQLite allows them; the refusal is the one the table was given.

prompt: Appending with an expected version, and letting the loser re-read, is called ___ concurrency.
Why must evolve never raise an exception for an event it dislikes?

choices.text: Exceptions are slow inside reduce
choices.why: Speed is beside the point; a raised exception would make the stream unreadable.

choices.text: Python forbids raising inside a match statement
choices.why: It allows it; the reason is about stored history, not syntax.

choices.text: A frozen dataclass cannot be returned after an exception
choices.why: Freezing concerns mutation, not exceptions; nothing about it stops a raise.

choices.text: The event is stored, so every later fold would fail on it
choices.why: Right. Events are facts; the rules belong in the command, before the event exists.

prompt: Put the steps of lend() in fold.py in order.
items: Fold them with evolve into a Member and a version
Check the rules against that state
trap: The state is computed before the rules and thrown away after; only the event is stored.

prompt: An auditor asks what Bia held on the day of her second event. With fold.py, how do you answer?

choices.text: Restore last month's database backup and look
choices.why: A backup shows one past moment at best; the events give every moment.

choices.text: Fold only the first two events
choices.why: Right. Stopping the fold early is the whole of time travel here.

choices.text: Read the Member row as it was stored at version 2
choices.why: No Member is stored at any version; the state is always worked out.

prompt: MostBorrowed was created after every loan had happened. How did it count them?

choices.text: It asked FinesOwed, which had seen them
choices.why: Projections do not read each other; FinesOwed ignores loans anyway.

choices.text: Lending kept a counter in case a screen ever wanted it
choices.why: No such counter exists, and with events kept none is needed.

choices.text: catch_up read the whole store from position 0
choices.why: Right. A new projection starts with a checkpoint of 0 and reads the whole history.

prompt: A projection computes "days overdue" with date.today(). What goes wrong?

choices.text: Each rebuild gives a different answer from the same events
choices.why: Right. A projection must be deterministic in the events; the date belongs in the event.

choices.text: date.today() is not allowed in threads
choices.why: It is; the problem is that the answer depends on when the rebuild runs.

choices.text: The checkpoint stops advancing
choices.why: The checkpoint moves as usual; the numbers it stands beside are what drift.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the server clock is correct
choices.why: A correct clock still reads a different day tomorrow, so a rebuild tomorrow disagrees with today's.

prompt: Match each projection rule to what breaking it would cause.

pairs.left: It never calls the write side for facts
pairs.right: the coupling the split removed comes back
a restart would not know where to resume

prompt: In snapshot.py, how many events did the rebuild apply when it started from the snapshot?
Once a snapshot exists at version 10,002, may the events before it be archived away?

choices.text: No: a snapshot is a cache, and the events are still the record
choices.why: Right. Deleting a snapshot loses nothing; deleting events loses history.

choices.text: Yes, the snapshot holds everything those earlier events said
choices.why: It holds one fold of them; projections, audits and a fixed evolve all need the events.

choices.text: Yes, if the snapshot is less than a year old
choices.why: Age is not the question; a snapshot is derived and the events are not.

prompt: A bug in evolve is fixed. Snapshots were taken while it lived. What should happen to them?

choices.text: Keep them: the next rebuild corrects them automatically
choices.why: The rebuild starts from the snapshot and folds only later events, so the wrong state survives.

choices.text: Edit them by hand to the right values
choices.why: Hand edits are guesses; folding from version 1 under the fixed code is exact.

choices.text: Delete them all and fold again under the fixed code
choices.why: Right. Snapshots are disposable by design; that is what makes the fix safe.

choices.text: Append correction events to every affected stream
choices.why: The events were right; only the cached fold was wrong.

prompt: In lag.py, why was the projection empty when read straight after Dani's return?

choices.text: The store had not committed the events yet
choices.why: append commits before it returns; the store was at position 2.

choices.text: FinesOwed ignores CopyReturned until a payment arrives
choices.why: It adds the fine on CopyReturned, as the next line shows.

choices.text: The worker had not applied them yet
choices.why: Right. The projection was at 0 while the store was at 2.

prompt: A worker applies event 41, then crashes before saving its checkpoint of 40. What happens on restart, and what must the projection tolerate?

choices.text: Event 41 is lost, so the projection must tolerate gaps
choices.why: It is still in the store; reading after 40 delivers it again.

choices.text: 41 is applied twice; repeats must be safe
choices.why: Right. Delivery is at least once, so save the checkpoint with the result or make apply idempotent.

choices.text: The store refuses to deliver event 41 twice
choices.why: The store does not know who read what; the checkpoint is the projection's business.

prompt: Match each number to what it says about a projection.

pairs.right: how many events it is behind

prompt: Old CopyLent events have no title. Why not run a migration that adds one to each stored row?

choices.text: Editing stored history breaks the store's one promise
choices.why: Right. An upcaster changes the reading and leaves the row as written; the trigger would refuse the edit anyway.

choices.text: SQLite cannot add keys to JSON text
choices.why: It can, with json_set; the reason is about history, not capability.

choices.text: The migration would be too slow on ten thousand rows
choices.why: Ten thousand rows update in moments; speed is not what forbids it.

prompt: The library starts charging fines in reais. What should happen to the fine field of CopyReturned?

choices.text: New events store reais in fine; readers divide old ones by 100
choices.why: Readers cannot tell old from new by the field, so sums mix cents and reais quietly.

choices.text: An upcaster that multiplies old fines by 100 on reading
choices.why: That turns correct old cents into wrong numbers; nothing about the old events changed.

choices.text: Rewrite the stored events in reais
choices.why: Stored events are never rewritten, and the trigger refuses it.

choices.text: A new field or type; fine keeps meaning cents
choices.why: Right. An event's meaning is fixed when written; only its shape may be adapted.

prompt: Which of these must be deterministic in the events they read? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: evolve
choices.why: Right. Every fold of the same stream must give the same state.

choices.text: A projection such as FinesOwed
choices.why: Right. A rebuild from 0 must reproduce the same read model.

choices.text: An upcaster such as lent_v1_to_v2
choices.why: Right. The same stored row must be read the same way forever, hence the frozen TITLE_OF.

choices.text: The lend command, deciding whether Bia may borrow
choices.why: A command may read the clock or other inputs; what it decides is recorded as an event, and the event is what later code reads.

prompt: Order these from cheapest to discard to most dangerous to discard.
trap: A projection costs a rebuild over the whole store, a snapshot only a longer fold; an event cannot be recovered at all.

prompt: A screen reads FinesOwed to decide whether to offer Bia the Lend button, and lend() refuses her anyway. Which is right?

choices.text: The screen, because the projection is newer than the command
choices.why: A projection is never newer than the store; at best it has caught up.

choices.text: lend(), because it folds her stream, which is the truth
choices.why: Right. The screen may be behind; the decision reads the events themselves.

choices.text: Neither until a snapshot is taken
choices.why: Snapshots only speed the fold up; the answer is the same without one.
